slides.title: Equations with Like Terms and the Distributive Property
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today: equations with like terms to collect and parentheses to distribute.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Q4 is where every equation today ends: once the like terms are collected and the parentheses gone, it is 1.03's two-step equation. Say that in one sentence after the reveal. The first class after Thanksgiving — two minutes silent, then reveal, no discussion.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Four words the notes use from the first line. Point at a coefficient, a constant and a pair of like terms in 8x − 4 + 2x as each is read. 'Distribute' means the number outside reaches every term inside — say 'every' twice.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
3x and 5x are like terms: three x's and five more x's are eight x's. The −4 is a constant and is not like either. Once the x-terms are collected the equation is Unit 1's two-step equation: add 4 to both sides, divide both sides by 8. A like term has the same letter to the same power — x and x² are not alike, and that is the only power we see this unit. The last line writes an equation from a story before board 7 asks for one: the \$9 is paid every week, so it multiplies w — the coefficient; the \$20 is paid once — the constant; the \$83 is the total. Do not solve it on the slide (w = 7); say only which number goes where and why.
OFF: 'Same letter, same power: they collect. A number on its own is a constant.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
The 3 multiplies the 2x AND the −5: 6x − 15. Then −15 and +4 are like terms (both constants): −11. Then two steps. A board that writes 6x − 5 has distributed to one term only — the B1G-M's first named misconception for this benchmark. The last line is the decimal the unit asks for every day: 0.5 of 10x is 5x and 0.5 of −4 is −2 — the decimal reaches both terms exactly as the 3 did (board 3 and set question 4 use it).
OFF: 'The number outside multiplies every term inside.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
The 3(x − 2) is subtracted, so the factor is −3, and it multiplies both terms: (−3)(x) = −3x and (−3)(−2) = +6. 18 + 6 = 24. Never 18 − 3 first: the 3 belongs to the parentheses, not to the 18. Then the check — put 5 back in the FIRST equation, not a later line: 18 − 3(5 − 2) = 18 − 9 = 9. Draw two arrows by hand from the −3, one to the x and one to the −2, and circle the −3 and the +6: the slide cannot (board 5 asks for exactly this line next).
OFF: 'The minus sign belongs to the 3. It goes in with it.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Ask which two terms are like terms before anyone writes: 5x and −2x. The 9 is a constant and waits.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: 5x − 2x = 3x (the minus belongs to the 2x). Then two steps: subtract 9, divide by 3. Check in the first equation: 35 + 9 − 14 = 30. A board with x = 3 collected 5x + 2x = 7x and then 7x = 21.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 7x − 4x = 3x, then add 3 and divide by 3: x = 9. This catches a student who watched the collecting without doing it — a board with 11x − 3 = 24 added the x-terms; one with x = 7 subtracted the 3.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Ask what the 5 multiplies before anyone writes: the x AND the −3.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: 5(x − 3) is 5x − 15. Then 5x and 2x are like terms: 7x. Two steps: add 15, divide by 7. Check: 5(8 − 3) + 16 = 25 + 16 = 41. A board with 7x − 3 = 41 distributed to one term.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 4x − 8 + 3x = 34, so 7x − 8 = 34 and x = 6. This catches the one-term distribution: a board with 7x − 2 = 34 gets 36/7, and one that never collects is stuck with two x-terms.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Collect, then one step. A board with x = 28 kept only the 2x; one with x ≈ 9.33 kept only the 6x. Check: 2(7) + 6(7) = 14 + 42 = 56.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: A different letter, the same move. A board with 13y + 3 = 48 added the 4y; one with y = 9.6 never took the 3 off.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Notes II's last line, used: 0.5 of 6n is 3n and 0.5 of 4 is 2. A board with n = 3.6 wrote 3n + 4 (the decimal to one term only — the state's most-missed skill); one with n = 20/3 left out the 2n. Check: 0.5(28) + 8 = 14 + 8 = 22.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. Option A is the one-term distribution, option C the sign, option B the lost x. On a split: sixty seconds, convince your neighbor, re-vote — then check 6 in the first equation: 2(7) + 6 = 20.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic, and Notes III's Your Turn: the same shape — a subtracted group with a minus inside, so (−3)(−4) = +12. Three named errors, each the next line a student really writes. Option C is the sign, option D subtracts before distributing, option A distributes to one term. Ask a room that chose B to finish it: 24 − 3x = 6, x = 6.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: The pattern breaks: the group is subtracted, but the inside term is +1, so (−2)(+1) = −2 — not the +6 of Notes III and +12 of board 5. A board with w = 6 wrote 15 − 2w + 2 (the Notes III pattern copied: the sign); one with w = 5.5 wrote 15 − 2w + 1 (one term). Check: 15 − 2(4 + 1) = 15 − 10 = 5.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: The extra-number board (ruling 22): Dana's age, 13, is not needed. Notes I's last line modeled this: the \$12 is paid every month — the coefficient; the \$25 once — the constant. Check: 25 + 12(6) = 97.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Backwards: the solution is given and a number in the equation is missing. Put 8 in for x, take off the 16, divide by 3. Check: 3(8 + 2) + 2(8) = 30 + 16 = 46.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written, and the exit evidence. Sam's work is printed as numbered lines so 'which line' has an answer: line 1. Read two aloud. Sam's wrong move gives 5.5, not 7, so a check of his answer exposes it: 4(5.5 − 2) + 3 = 17, not 23.
